MOCK CLAT 10025 (ESSENTIAL)
ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
English Language
1.	Answer: A
Passage 1 Summary — Nietzsche and the “Will to Power”
The passage argues that human desires, impulses, and will may provide the foundation for
understanding all reality, including the mechanical world. The author rejects the idea of separating
material processes from emotional or instinctive life and instead proposes that a single principle of
causality should explain existence. This methodological approach leads to the hypothesis that all active
force ultimately derives from “Will to Power.” Mechanical action, biological functions, and organic
development are interpreted as manifestations of this underlying will. Thus, the passage presents a
philosophical attempt to unify reality through one central motivating force rather than multiple
independent causes.
Difficulty Level: Hard
Lines of Reference: o “whether this which is ‘given’ does not SUFFICE... for the understanding even
of the so-called mechanical world”
o “whether all mechanical action... is not just the power of will”
o “define ALL active force unequivocally as WILL TO POWER”
Explanation: Option (A) — Correct
defending the claim that all forms of causality may ultimately be reduced to a single
underlying principle of will.
This option most accurately captures the central philosophical movement of the passage. The author
begins by questioning whether the world of desires, passions, and impulses may itself suffice for
understanding even the so-called mechanical or material world. From there, the argument develops
methodically toward the idea that explanatory systems should avoid multiplying causes unnecessarily.
This “morality of method” leads the author to propose that will itself may constitute the only genuine
form of causality. The culmination of the passage appears in the concept of the “Will to Power,” which
the author presents as the possible underlying force governing both organic life and mechanical
activity. Thus, the passage consistently seeks to unify apparently different forms of causation within a
single explanatory principle centered upon will.
Option (B)
criticizing materialist philosophy for denying the emotional foundations underlying human
consciousness and perception.
This option appears plausible because the passage repeatedly privileges impulses, desires, and
emotions as philosophically significant realities. Readers may therefore infer that the author’s primary
target is materialist philosophy. However, the passage does not mainly criticize materialism for
misunderstanding consciousness or emotional life. Instead, the author uses emotional and instinctive
reality as the starting point for a broader metaphysical argument concerning causality itself. The
emphasis lies not on defending consciousness psychologically, but on proposing a unified explanatory
principle connecting both material and organic existence. Therefore, the option narrows the argument
excessively toward criticism of materialism.
Option (C)
explaining why mechanical interpretations of reality fail to account adequately for
biological development and instinct.

This option sounds convincing because the passage discusses instinctive life, organic functions,
nutrition, assimilation, and the branching of organic processes from a more primitive unity. Readers
may therefore interpret the argument as mainly biological. However, biological discussion serves only
as supporting evidence within a larger metaphysical framework. The author is less interested in
disproving mechanical explanations biologically than in redefining causality philosophically through
the concept of will. The passage ultimately aims to reinterpret all active force—not merely organic
development—through the “Will to Power.” Thus, the option captures one dimension of the argument
while missing its broader metaphysical scope.
Option (D)
demonstrating that philosophical inquiry becomes incoherent whenever it separates
emotion from rational thought.
This option is incorrect because the passage does not primarily concern the relationship between
emotion and rationality. Although impulses and passions are treated as foundational realities, the
author never argues directly that separating emotion from reason makes philosophy incoherent.
Instead, the passage focuses on causality, metaphysics, and the possibility of reducing all forms of force
to will. Rational inquiry itself remains important throughout the argument, especially in the discussion
of “logical method.” Therefore, the option imposes a psychological conflict between emotion and
rationality that the passage does not centrally develop.
2.	Answer: B
Difficulty Level: Moderate-Hard
Lines of Reference: o “Not to assume several kinds of causality...”
o “the attempt to get along with a single one has not been pushed to its furthest extent”
o “that is a morality of method”
Explanation: Option (A)
philosophical systems should avoid speculative reasoning unsupported by direct empirical
verification.
This option appears plausible because the passage repeatedly refers to “logical method” and attempts to
ground philosophical reasoning systematically rather than arbitrarily. Readers may therefore infer that
the author advocates empirical caution. However, the passage is fundamentally speculative and
metaphysical in nature. The author openly constructs hypothetical arguments concerning will,
causality, and the “Will to Power” without relying upon empirical verification in the scientific sense.
The “morality of method” does not reject speculation; rather, it regulates how explanatory principles
should be introduced. Thus, the option incorrectly interprets the author as advocating strict empiricism
instead of methodological economy.
Option (B) — Correct
intellectual inquiry must exhaust unified explanations before introducing multiple
explanatory causes.
This option most accurately captures the meaning of the phrase within the passage. The author
explicitly states that one should not “assume several kinds of causality” until the attempt to explain
phenomena through a single form of causality has been pushed to its furthest extent. This
methodological principle is what the author calls a “morality of method.” The argument therefore favors
explanatory unity and conceptual economy rather than unnecessary multiplication of causes. From this
principle, the author proceeds toward the hypothesis that will itself may represent the only genuine
causality underlying both organic and mechanical processes. Thus, the phrase refers specifically to
disciplined intellectual inquiry seeking the simplest and most unified explanatory framework possible.
Option (C)

logical consistency becomes possible only when emotional experience is treated as
philosophically primary.
This option sounds convincing because the passage begins by treating desires, passions, and impulses
as the only realities genuinely “given.” Readers may therefore infer that emotional experience forms the
basis of logical consistency itself. However, the “morality of method” does not specifically concern
emotional primacy. Instead, it concerns methodological discipline regarding causality and explanation.
The author’s point is not that logic depends upon emotions, but that inquiry should avoid multiplying
explanatory principles prematurely. Therefore, the option confuses the passage’s starting point—the
reality of impulses—with the methodological principle being discussed later.
Option (D)
scientific reasoning should remain independent from metaphysical assumptions concerning
will and causality.
This option is incorrect because the passage argues almost the opposite. The author explicitly attempts
to extend the concept of will into a universal explanatory principle governing causality itself. Rather
than separating scientific or logical reasoning from metaphysical assumptions, the passage integrates
them closely. The “morality of method” is used precisely to justify a metaphysical hypothesis about will
operating as the only causality. Therefore, the option directly contradicts the argumentative direction of
the passage.
3.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Hard
Lines of Reference: e “we MUST make the attempt to posit hypothetically the causality of the will as
the only causality”
e “whether all mechanical action... is not just the power of will”
Explanation: Option (A) — Correct
Mechanical explanations of reality remain incomplete if they exclude the possibility of
underlying purposive force.
This option most accurately reflects the deeper philosophical implication developed across the passage.
The author repeatedly questions whether the so-called “mechanical” or “material” world can truly be
understood independently of will, impulse, and purposive activity. The argument gradually advances
toward the hypothesis that all forms of causality may ultimately derive from will itself. By proposing
that even mechanical action may simply be “the power of will, the effect of will,” the author suggests
that purely mechanical explanations fail to account for the deeper operative principle underlying
activity and force. Thus, the passage implies that material explanations alone remain incomplete if they
exclude the possibility of an underlying purposive or volitional basis structuring reality.
Option (B)
Human understanding of causality depends primarily upon the reliability of sensory and
material observation.
This option appears plausible because the passage is deeply concerned with causality and attempts to
establish a systematic method for understanding reality. Readers may therefore assume the author
grounds causality in observable material evidence. However, the passage explicitly distances itself from
purely sensory or material explanation. The author begins not with external observation, but with the
“world of desires and passions” as the only genuinely “given” reality. The argument proceeds
metaphysically rather than empirically, attempting to reinterpret material processes through will
rather than through sensory verification. Therefore, the option imposes an empirical framework the
passage consistently moves beyond.
Option (C)

Organic life gradually emerged through the separation of instinctive unity into distinct
physiological functions.
This option sounds convincing because the passage discusses a “primary form of life” in which functions
such as nutrition, secretion, assimilation, and self-regulation remain synthetically united before
branching into differentiated processes. Readers may therefore infer a developmental account of
biological complexity emerging from primitive unity. However, the passage introduces this idea mainly
as supporting illustration rather than as its principal implication. The author’s larger concern is
metaphysical unification through will and causality, not biological evolution itself. Thus, while the
statement reflects one aspect of the discussion, it does not represent the strongest implied philosophical
conclusion of the passage.
Option (D)
Philosophical accounts of reality inevitably collapse when they attempt to explain emotion
materially.
This option is incorrect because the passage never argues that philosophical systems collapse through
material explanations of emotion. In fact, the author attempts almost the reverse movement: explaining
the material world itself through concepts associated with impulse, desire, and will. The argument
seeks continuity between emotional and material reality rather than conflict between them. Therefore,
the option introduces a claim about philosophical failure that the passage neither develops nor implies
strongly.
4.	Answer: C
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Lines of Reference: e “Supposing that nothing else is ‘given’...”
e “Granted, finally...”
e Entire hypothetical progression leading toward “Will to Power”
Explanation: Option (A)
distance the argument from definitive philosophical commitment by emphasizing
uncertainty and abstraction.
This option appears plausible because the passage repeatedly employs speculative and conditional
language rather than asserting conclusions dogmatically. Readers may therefore interpret the author
as deliberately avoiding firm philosophical commitment. However, the conditional structure does not
primarily function as hesitation or withdrawal from the argument. Instead, the author uses
hypothetical reasoning strategically to guide readers step by step toward a broader metaphysical
conclusion concerning will and causality. The speculative tone therefore supports argumentative
progression rather than intellectual detachment. Thus, the option mistakes methodological construction
for philosophical uncertainty.
Option (B)
contrast speculative metaphysical reasoning against the methodological certainty
associated with mathematics.
This option sounds convincing because the passage briefly refers to mathematics while discussing the
“morality of method,” which may suggest comparison between philosophical speculation and
mathematical rigor. Readers may therefore infer that the author contrasts uncertain metaphysical
inquiry against scientific or mathematical certainty. However, the mathematical reference serves only
to reinforce the author’s methodological principle regarding explanatory economy. The repeated
conditional constructions themselves are not primarily designed to contrast philosophy with
mathematics. Instead, they organize the development of the hypothesis systematically. Therefore, the

option overemphasizes a minor reference within the passage while overlooking the broader
argumentative structure.
Option (C) — Correct
construct a hypothetical sequence of reasoning leading progressively toward a unified
explanatory conclusion.
This option most accurately captures the rhetorical and logical function of the conditional constructions.
The author deliberately builds the argument through successive hypothetical stages: first questioning
whether desires and impulses might suffice for understanding reality, then proposing will as the only
genuine form of causality, and finally extending this reasoning toward the “Will to Power” as the
underlying basis of all active force. Expressions such as “Supposing that...” and “Granted, finally...”
therefore serve as intellectual transitions within a carefully layered chain of reasoning. Each
conditional step advances the argument closer to a comprehensive explanatory conclusion regarding the
nature of reality and causality. The passage’s structure is therefore cumulative and progressive rather
than uncertain or merely speculative.
Option (D)
demonstrate that philosophical systems become persuasive only when grounded in
empirical scientific evidence.
This option is incorrect because the passage does not rely primarily upon empirical scientific evidence.
The author openly constructs a speculative metaphysical argument based upon logical and
methodological principles rather than experimental proof. The conditional structures are used to extend
philosophical reasoning hypothetically, not to establish empirical verification. Therefore, the option
imposes a scientific framework inconsistent with the passage’s speculative metaphysical style.
5.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Hard
Lines of Reference: © “The world seen from within”
o “the world defined and designated according to its ‘intelligible character”
o “it would simply be ‘Will to Power,’ and nothing else.”
Explanation: Option (A) — Correct
interpreting reality according to its underlying motivating force rather than merely its
external appearance.
This option most accurately captures the meaning of the phrase within the philosophical framework of
the passage. Throughout the argument, the author attempts to move beyond surface-level mechanical
explanations of reality toward a deeper causal principle grounded in will. By the concluding lines, the
“world seen from within” refers not to the externally observable material world alone, but to reality
understood through its inner operative force—namely the “Will to Power.” The contrast is therefore
between external appearances or mechanical descriptions and the deeper motivating principle
underlying all activity and force. Thus, the phrase signifies an interpretative shift from outward
phenomena toward internal causality and intelligible character.
Option (B)
understanding existence primarily through subjective emotional and psychological states of
consciousness.
This option appears plausible because the passage begins by treating desires, passions, and impulses as
the only genuinely “given” reality. Readers may therefore infer that “from within” refers mainly to
subjective emotional consciousness. However, the phrase ultimately functions more broadly than
individual psychology. The author is not merely privileging subjective experience, but attempting to
reinterpret all reality—including mechanical and material processes—through an underlying principle

of will. Thus, while emotional and instinctive experience forms the starting point of the argument, the
phrase refers more fundamentally to inner causality rather than personal psychology alone.
Option (C)
rejecting scientific explanations of reality in favour of instinctive and intuitive forms of
knowledge.
This option sounds convincing because the passage challenges mechanical explanations and elevates
instinctive life philosophically. Readers may therefore assume the author rejects scientific reasoning
altogether. However, the passage does not dismiss explanation systematically; instead, it proposes a
different explanatory principle. In fact, the author repeatedly emphasizes “logical method” and
disciplined causality. The argument seeks metaphysical unification rather than anti-scientific
intuitionism. Therefore, the option exaggerates the opposition between instinct and _ scientific
explanation beyond what the passage supports.
Option (D)
examining the internal structure of human cognition independently from material and
biological processes.
This option is incorrect because the passage does not isolate human cognition from biology or material
existence. On the contrary, the author attempts to connect organic functions, instinctive life, material
processes, and will within a unified explanatory framework. The phrase “the world seen from within”
refers to reality understood through its operative force, not to an independent analysis of cognition
separated from bodily or material processes. Therefore, the option narrows the phrase excessively
toward psychology and epistemology while ignoring the broader metaphysical argument.
6.	Answer: B
Passage 2 Summary — Social Media and Modern Communication
The passage examines the paradoxical nature of social media in contemporary society. While these
platforms claim to promote connection, democratic participation, and public awareness, they often
intensify isolation, misinformation, and emotional extremity. The author explores the contradiction
between increased expression and declining meaningful dialogue, suggesting that the deeper problem
may not lie in technology itself but in the human impulses amplified through it. Emotional outrage
frequently overshadows thoughtful reflection, making truth difficult to distinguish amid informational
noise. Ultimately, the passage presents social media as both empowering and damaging, raising
philosophical questions about communication, responsibility, and society’s weakening capacity for
restraint and critical thinking.
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Lines of Reference: o Contrast between “greater connection” and increasing isolation
o References to weakened meaningful dialogue despite expanded communication
Explanation: Option A: Technological freedom often weakens institutional authority. —
Incorrect
This option appears attractive because the first speaker’s statement — “Social media gave ordinary
people a voice” — does suggest the democratisation of communication. The passage also reinforces this
idea by describing social media as “a democratic space where the powerless can challenge authority and
reshape public discourse.” Therefore, a student reading quickly may assume that the central issue
concerns the weakening of traditional institutions and authority structures. However, this
interpretation remains incomplete because it ignores the second half of the contrast: “everyone screams
while nobody listens.” The discussion is not ultimately about authority losing power; rather, it is about
the quality of communication deteriorating despite greater participation. The author is less concerned
with institutional decline and more concerned with the paradox that increased expression may

simultaneously produce confusion, emotional noise, and the collapse of meaningful dialogue. Thus,
while the option contains an idea present in the passage, it does not capture the primary contradiction
reflected in the cartoon and passage together. It therefore becomes a close but incomplete trap option.
Option B: Increased participation in discourse does not necessarily improve meaningful
communication. — Correct
This option most accurately captures the philosophical contradiction presented in both the cartoon and
the passage. The statement “gave ordinary people a voice” symbolises broader participation,
accessibility, and democratic expression in modern communication. However, the response “everyone
screams while nobody listens” introduces the central irony: the expansion of voices has not necessarily
resulted in understanding, reflection, or productive dialogue. Instead, communication becomes
emotionally overwhelming and fragmented. This directly parallels the passage’s claim that social media
“amplifies voices, yet simultaneously drowns truth in noise.” The author repeatedly explores the
paradoxical nature of social media by showing that greater expression may coexist with declining
meaningful engagement. Importantly, the option remains balanced and analytical rather than extreme.
It neither completely condemns nor glorifies social media. Instead, it focuses on the deeper
communicative failure emerging within public discourse. Unlike the other choices, this option
successfully integrates both parts of the contrast — democratic participation and communicative
breakdown — making it the most comprehensive and textually accurate answer.
Option C: Social media users are primarily motivated by emotional insecurity and public
validation. — Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it introduces a psychological interpretation that extends beyond the
textual evidence provided in the cartoon and passage. The passage certainly criticises social media for
rewarding “emotional extremity over thoughtful reflection,” which suggests that emotionally charged
behaviour often dominates online discourse. However, the author never specifically claims that users
are “primarily motivated” by insecurity or the need for validation. Similarly, the cartoon focuses on the
broader social consequences of communication overload and lack of meaningful listening rather than on
individual emotional psychology. This option becomes a sophisticated trap because it sounds
intellectually plausible and aligns loosely with common criticisms of social media culture. However,
strong reading comprehension requires distinguishing between ideas that are directly supported and
ideas that are merely speculative extensions. The passage remains philosophical and societal in focus
rather than psychological. By shifting attention toward individual emotional motives, this option
overinterprets the author’s argument and introduces concepts not explicitly developed in the discussion.
Option D: Democratic participation inevitably produces ideological conflict and social
fragmentation. — Incorrect
This option is tempting because the cartoon itself presents disagreement and the passage discusses
conflicting perspectives surrounding social media. A reader may therefore assume that the author is
arguing that democratic participation naturally leads to division and fragmentation. However, the
keyword “inevitably” makes the statement excessively absolute and therefore inaccurate. The passage
does not suggest that democratic expression always results in ideological conflict. Instead, the author
argues that social media magnifies pre-existing human tendencies such as outrage, impulsiveness, and
lack of restraint. The focus is therefore on human behaviour and communicative quality rather than on
democracy itself being inherently destructive. Moreover, the primary contrast in the cartoon concerns
the paradox of increased expression without meaningful listening, not the inevitability of social
fragmentation. This option works as a strong trap because it contains elements genuinely connected to
the passage — disagreement, democracy, and conflict — but subtly shifts the central focus away from
communication failure toward political determinism. As a result, it misrepresents the author’s broader
philosophical argument.

7.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Moderate—Hard
Lines of Reference: © “emotional outrage frequently overshadows thoughtful reflection”
o discussion of amplified reactions and informational chaos
Explanation: Option A: One views social media primarily through its social possibilities,
while the other emphasises its psychological and communicative failures. — Correct
This option correctly captures the deeper contrast between the two speakers in both the cartoon and the
passage. The first speaker highlights the empowering and democratic dimensions of social media by
stating that it “gave ordinary people a voice” and helped expose injustice. This perspective aligns with
the passage’s description of social media as “a democratic space where the powerless can challenge
authority and reshape public discourse.” The second speaker, however, focuses on the destructive
consequences of the same system by arguing that “everyone screams while nobody listens” and that
“outrage spreads faster than truth.” These statements reflect concerns regarding emotional excess,
communicative breakdown, and distortion of truth — ideas directly connected to the passage’s criticism
that social media “rewards emotional extremity over thoughtful reflection.” Importantly, this option
remains broad and balanced enough to include both social and psychological dimensions without
becoming overly extreme. It accurately reflects the nuanced disagreement between optimism about
participation and concern about communicative deterioration.
Option B: One believes technology should be regulated, whereas the other opposes all forms
of digital censorship. — Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it introduces a debate about regulation and censorship that never
explicitly occurs in either the cartoon or the passage. While the speakers clearly disagree about the
consequences of social media, neither of them discusses government intervention, policy-making, or
digital restrictions. The first speaker defends the social utility of these platforms by emphasising
awareness and democratic participation, while the second criticises their emotional and communicative
consequences. However, disagreement about effects should not automatically be interpreted as
disagreement about regulation. This option becomes a strong trap because many contemporary debates
surrounding social media naturally involve censorship, platform moderation, and technological
regulation. A student relying on outside knowledge rather than textual evidence may therefore choose
this option impulsively. However, careful reading reveals that the conversation remains philosophical
and societal rather than political or legislative. Reading comprehension questions require students to
remain within the scope of the text instead of importing broader real-world debates into the passage.
Option C: One considers social media politically dangerous, while the other sees it as
economically exploitative. — Incorrect
This option misrepresents the actual focus of the disagreement by forcing it into political and economic
categories that are not central to the cartoon discussion. The second speaker certainly criticises the
spread of outrage and misinformation, which may indirectly relate to political consequences, but the
criticism is fundamentally about communication quality and emotional behaviour rather than political
danger itself. Similarly, the passage does mention that social media “commodifies attention,” which
introduces an economic dimension. However, neither speaker explicitly frames the debate in terms of
commercial exploitation or economic systems. The disagreement is broader and more philosophical:
whether social media empowers society or intensifies harmful human tendencies. This option becomes a
subtle trap because it uses sophisticated vocabulary directly taken from the passage, especially the idea
of commodification. However, it selectively isolates one aspect of the passage while ignoring the larger
communicative and psychological conflict. Therefore, the option sounds intellectually convincing but
ultimately distorts the central disagreement between the speakers.

Option D: One argues that social media spreads misinformation, while the other denies that
misinformation exists online. — Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it exaggerates the disagreement between the two speakers and creates
a false binary. The second speaker clearly believes that misinformation and outrage spread rapidly
online, especially through the statement “outrage spreads faster than truth.” However, the first speaker
never denies the existence of misinformation. Instead, the first speaker argues that social media also
creates awareness and gives marginalised individuals a platform to speak. The disagreement therefore
concerns the overall consequences and value of social media rather than the factual existence of
misinformation itself. This option becomes a trap because it simplifies a nuanced philosophical
disagreement into a rigid factual dispute. Many students may incorrectly assume that because one
speaker highlights benefits, that speaker must completely reject criticisms. However, the passage itself
maintains complexity and balance by presenting social media as simultaneously empowering and
harmful. The author deliberately avoids absolute positions, making this extreme interpretation
inconsistent with the overall tone and structure of the discussion.
8.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Lines of Reference: e suggestion that technology amplifies existing human impulses
e “the deeper problem may not lie in technology itself”
Explanation: Option A: manipulates perception by rewarding emotional extremity over
thoughtful reflection. — Correct
This option directly connects the cartoon statement with the author’s larger philosophical argument in
the passage. The line “outrage spreads faster than truth” suggests that emotionally provocative content
gains greater attention, visibility, and engagement than calm, rational, or carefully verified
information. This idea closely mirrors the passage’s criticism that social media “rewards emotional
extremity over thoughtful reflection.” The author argues that digital platforms amplify emotional
reactions because outrage attracts immediate attention and rapid circulation. As a result, perception
becomes distorted, not necessarily through direct censorship or lies, but through systems that prioritise
emotionally stimulating content over nuanced thinking. The phrase “manipulates perception” is
therefore important because the distortion occurs indirectly through incentive structures and patterns
of engagement. This option successfully integrates both the communicative and psychological
dimensions of the passage. Unlike the other options, it remains closely tied to the exact wording and
conceptual framework of the text without introducing exaggerated or unrelated claims.
Option B: encourages individuals to reject all forms of intellectual disagreement. —
Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it overstates the consequences of outrage-driven communication. The
cartoon statement suggests that emotionally charged content spreads rapidly and often dominates
discourse, but it does not imply that individuals reject all forms of disagreement. The use of absolute
language such as “all forms” makes the option excessively broad and therefore inconsistent with the
nuanced tone of the passage. The author criticises the decline of thoughtful reflection and meaningful
dialogue, yet nowhere claims that social media completely destroys intellectual engagement or rational
disagreement. In fact, the passage acknowledges that these platforms also create spaces for
participation and public discourse. This option becomes a sophisticated trap because it sounds
intellectually plausible and aligns with common criticisms of online culture. However, strong reading
comprehension requires attention to degree and scope. The passage presents social media as
paradoxical and complex rather than entirely destructive. By turning a partial tendency into a
universal conclusion, this option exaggerates the author’s argument beyond the textual evidence.

Option C: weakens democracy by eliminating rational political participation entirely. —
Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it introduces an extreme political conclusion not supported by the
passage. While the statement “outrage spreads faster than truth” certainly implies that emotional
reactions often dominate public discourse, the author never argues that rational political participation
has been entirely eliminated. In fact, the passage explicitly acknowledges the democratic potential of
social media by describing it as “a democratic space where the powerless can challenge authority and
reshape public discourse.” Therefore, the author does not present social media as wholly destructive to
democracy. Instead, the passage explores the tension between empowerment and distortion. This option
becomes a close trap because it draws from genuine concerns raised in the passage — misinformation,
emotionality, and manipulation — but exaggerates them into a total collapse of rational democratic
participation. The word “entirely” is especially important because it transforms a nuanced critique into
an absolute judgment. Careful readers must recognise that the author maintains balance throughout
the discussion rather than endorsing complete technological pessimism.
Option D: transforms public discourse into commercially controlled propaganda. —
Incorrect
This option is tempting because the passage includes the phrase “commodifies attention,” which
introduces an economic dimension to the critique of social media. A reader may therefore associate
outrage and misinformation with commercial motives such as profit generation and audience
manipulation. However, the statement “outrage spreads faster than truth” primarily concerns emotional
amplification and communicative distortion rather than organised propaganda or direct commercial
control. The author critiques how social media rewards emotional extremity, but does not explicitly
argue that all public discourse becomes propaganda controlled by commercial forces. This option subtly
shifts the focus from psychological and social consequences toward political-economic control
mechanisms. While commercial incentives may indirectly contribute to outrage-driven systems, the
central concern in the passage remains the broader philosophical issue of human behaviour, attention,
and critical thinking. Therefore, this option contains a partially relevant idea but ultimately
misrepresents the passage by narrowing the argument into an overly political and commercial
interpretation.
9.	Answer: A
Difficulty Level: Hard
Lines of Reference: ¢ metaphorical descriptions of “noise, »« chaos,” and informational overload
e emotionally charged language surrounding communication breakdown
Explanation: Option A: factual accuracy becomes difficult to recognise amid excessive
emotional and informational stimulation. — Correct
This option most accurately captures the meaning of the phrase “drowns truth in noise” in the context of
both the cartoon and the passage. The author is not arguing that truth completely disappears online,
but rather that it becomes increasingly difficult to identify amid overwhelming quantities of emotional
reactions, opinions, outrage, misinformation, and rapid digital engagement. The cartoon reinforces this
interpretation through the line “outrage spreads faster than truth,” which implies that emotionally
charged content gains more attention than careful or factual discussion. The passage similarly criticises
social media for rewarding “emotional extremity over thoughtful reflection.” Together, these ideas
suggest that excessive informational and emotional stimulation creates confusion, distraction, and
distortion. The phrase “noise” symbolises communicative overload rather than literal sound. This option
succeeds because it preserves the philosophical and communicative focus of the passage without

becoming excessively political or extreme. It also recognises that the problem lies not merely in
falsehood itself, but in society’s declining ability to distinguish thoughtful truth from emotional chaos.
Option B: truthful information is deliberately hidden by digital corporations and
governments. — Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it introduces the idea of deliberate suppression and organised
concealment, which is never explicitly suggested in either the cartoon or the passage. The phrase
“drowns truth in noise” refers to truth becoming obscured by excessive emotional reactions, conflicting
opinions, and overwhelming information, not by intentional censorship. Similarly, the cartoon
statement “outrage spreads faster than truth” implies imbalance in attention and engagement rather
than coordinated hiding of factual information. This option becomes a strong trap because many real-
world debates about social media involve corporate algorithms, censorship, and governmental control. A
student relying on outside assumptions rather than textual evidence may therefore select it quickly.
However, the author’s focus remains philosophical and communicative rather than conspiratorial or
institutional. The passage critiques the structure of online discourse and human behavioural tendencies
rather than accusing corporations or governments of intentionally concealing truth. Thus, the option
shifts the discussion away from communicative overload toward political manipulation, which exceeds
the actual scope of the text.
Option C: social media encourages individuals to distrust all forms of public
communication. — Incorrect
This option is incorrect because it exaggerates the consequences of misinformation and emotional
overload presented in the passage. The phrase “drowns truth in noise” certainly suggests confusion and
difficulty in identifying reliable information, but it does not imply that people completely lose trust in
all forms of public communication. The author maintains a balanced and analytical tone throughout the
passage by acknowledging both the empowering and damaging dimensions of social media. Similarly,
the cartoon discussion reflects disagreement about consequences rather than complete communicative
collapse. The use of the phrase “all forms” makes the option excessively absolute and therefore
inconsistent with the nuanced argument of the passage. This option becomes a subtle trap because it
extends a partially reasonable inference — declining trust and communicative confusion — into a
universal conclusion. Strong reading comprehension requires students to distinguish between broad
tendencies and absolute claims. The author critiques the distortion of meaningful dialogue but does not
claim that society has become entirely incapable of trusting communication itself.
Option D: online discussions are generally louder and more chaotic than physical

Explanation: Argument I: "Extended compulsory education will automatically generate
higher graduate employment rates and substantially reduce youth unemployment across all
demographic groups." (Weak argument — relies on an unsubstantiated causal chain
connecting extended schooling to employment outcomes through the logically unsupported
word "automatically"). The argument presumes a direct, self-executing relationship between years of
compulsory schooling and employment generation that economic evidence does not support. Graduate
unemployment in India is structurally high, and simply extending the duration of compulsory
education without addressing curriculum relevance, pedagogical quality, and labour market absorption
capacity would not produce the outcomes asserted. The qualifier "automatically" is particularly fatal to
this argument's validity — employment outcomes depend on a complex interaction of economic
conditions, skill alignment, and industrial demand that no educational mandate can independently
guarantee. The argument mistakes policy intent for policy effect.
Argument II: "India's existing school infrastructure, teacher availability, and retention
mechanisms remain critically inadequate to meaningfully support compulsory schooling
beyond current mandated levels." (Strong argument — identifies concrete, systemic, and
empirically documented structural constraints that directly undermine the feasibility of the
proposed extension). This argument's strength lies in its diagnostic precision. India's dropout rates
are already significant well before Class VIII in several states, and teacher vacancy figures,
particularly at the secondary level, remain consistently unaddressed. Extending compulsion without
first remedying these foundational deficiencies would create a legal mandate unsupported by
operational capacity — producing coerced enrolment without commensurate educational attainment.
The argument directly engages the policy's implementability rather than its desirability in the
abstract, which is the appropriate analytical standard for evaluating practical policy proposals. It
identifies the prerequisite conditions that must precede rather than follow such an extension.
Argument III: "Nations maintaining compulsory education until age 18 consistently
demonstrate higher Human Development Index rankings than countries with shorter
mandatory schooling periods." (Weak argument — commits the classic error of inferring
causation from correlation without controlling for confounding developmental variables).
HDI rankings are composite outcomes shaped by healthcare systems, income distribution, gender
equity, governance quality, and economic growth trajectories — none of which this argument accounts
for. Nations with higher HDI rankings typically also have superior infrastructure, better funded
institutions, and more equitable resource distribution, any of which might independently explain both
their educational policy ambitions and their HDI performance. The argument cannot isolate
compulsory schooling duration as the determinative variable. Furthermore, cross-national comparisons
fail to account for the vastly different starting conditions between India and higher-HDI nations,
making direct policy inference methodologically unsound.

Explanation: Argument I: "Compulsory voting infringes upon the constitutionally protected
right to freedom of expression, which inherently encompasses the right to withhold
electoral participation as a form of political dissent." (Strong argument — raises a
substantive constitutional objection grounded in established legal doctrine and the
recognised negative dimension of fundamental rights). The argument correctly invokes the
negative liberty dimension of Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution, under which the freedom of
expression has been judicially interpreted to include the freedom not to speak or participate. The right
to abstain from voting as an act of political protest or principled non-participation is not merely
theoretical — it has been recognised in democratic jurisprudence globally as a legitimate expressive
act. Mandating electoral participation compels citizens to engage with a process they may
conscientiously reject, which constitutes a cognisable restriction on expressive freedom. The argument's
grounding in constitutional principle — rather than mere preference — gives it analytical strength that
policy convenience cannot easily override.
Argument II: "Australia's sustained experience with mandatory voting demonstrates that
compelled participation eliminates voter suppression tactics and produces elected
governments with substantially broader democratic legitimacy." (Weak argument — draws
an inapposite cross-national comparison without accounting for foundational
constitutional, demographic, and institutional differences between Australia and India).
Australia's compulsory voting model operates within a Westminster parliamentary tradition, a
comparatively compact and literate electorate, a robust fine-enforcement mechanism, and
constitutional arrangements that differ fundamentally from India's federal complexity and scale.
Transposing this experience to India — with its 970 million registered voters, multilingual diversity,
widespread infrastructural unevenness, and deeply differentiated civic access conditions — without
demonstrating structural comparability is methodologically inadequate. Furthermore, the claim that
mandatory voting "eliminates voter suppression" conflates the distinct problems of disengagement and
coercive disenfranchisement, which have different causal origins and require distinct remedial
responses. Participation rates alone do not establish democratic legitimacy if the quality of informed,
voluntary electoral choice is simultaneously undermined.
Argument III: "Declining voter turnout reflects deepening citizen disillusionment with
electoral processes, which coercive participation mandates cannot address without prior
structural reforms to electoral accountability mechanisms." (Strong argument — correctly
diagnoses turnout decline as a symptomatic rather than originary problem, and
persuasively contests mandatory voting as a sufficient or appropriately targeted remedy).
This argument demonstrates sophisticated policy reasoning by distinguishing between the symptom —
declining turnout — and its structural causes — institutional mistrust, perceived electoral
unaccountability, and disillusionment with the representational system. Mandating participation
addresses the metric without addressing its underlying determinants, analogous to compelling
attendance at an institution whose credibility has eroded without restoring the institutional conditions
that generated trust. Coerced participation may produce numerical turnout without producing
informed, voluntary democratic engagement, which is the normative objective that turnout statistics
are intended to measure. The argument correctly identifies that the sequence matters — structural
reform must precede or accompany participation mandates for the policy to achieve its democratic
purpose rather than merely satisfying a quantitative threshold.
